pages.x: From the 1100s, Shona-speaking people on the high plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers built a city on and around a granite hill. Its name may come from dzimba dza mabwe, houses of stone. At its height, in the 1300s, perhaps 10,000 to 18,000 people lived there.
Its builders split granite into neat blocks and laid them without mortar. The outer wall of the Great Enclosure runs 250 metres and stands up to 11 metres high.
pages.fx: It is the largest ancient stone structure south of the Sahara. Inside stands a solid cone-shaped tower 9 metres high, whose purpose no one knows.

pages.x: The city grew rich on cattle and on gold from the mines of the plateau, carried to Kilwa and other Swahili ports on the Indian Ocean. In its ruins archaeologists found Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and glass beads from India.
Eight birds carved from soapstone, each on a tall pillar, were found at the site, perhaps standing for the spirits of royal ancestors. One of them is on the flag of Zimbabwe.

In the 1400s the city was left, perhaps because too many people and cattle had worn out the land, or because the gold trade moved north. Its power passed to new kingdoms such as Mutapa, which the Portuguese met in the 1500s.

When Europeans saw the ruins in the 1870s, many refused to believe that Africans had built them and credited the Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba. Archaeologists showed in 1905 and 1929 that the builders were ancestors of the Shona, but white-ruled Rhodesia kept up the lie into the 1970s.

Great Zimbabwe shows a rich African state trading across the Indian Ocean centuries before Europeans came. When Rhodesia became independent under majority rule in 1980, it took the city's name: Zimbabwe.
